title: Attention Is All You Need
description: The paper introducing the transformer, an architecture based entirely on attention mechanisms, removing recurrence and convolution from sequence transduction models.
quality_notes: The arXiv page states no venue, so we do not record one. Widely cited is not the same as confirmed peer reviewed.
why_useful: The primary source for the architecture underneath nearly everything current. Short, and far more readable after an illustrated explainer than before one.
learning_outcomes: Read the original formulation of scaled dot-product attention
Understand the encoder-decoder design as originally proposed
Distinguish the paper's actual claims from later folklore
abstract_summary: The abstract states that dominant sequence transduction models were built on recurrent or convolutional encoder-decoder networks, with the best also connecting encoder and decoder through attention. It proposes the Transformer, an architecture based solely on attention that dispenses with recurrence and convolution entirely, and reports that on two machine translation tasks these models were better in quality while being more parallelisable and needing significantly less time to train.
key_idea: Attention alone is enough to model sequence dependencies, and removing recurrence is what makes training parallelisable. That parallelism, rather than the attention mechanism by itself, is arguably why the architecture went on to dominate.

title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
description: The paper introducing BERT, a bidirectional transformer encoder pretrained on unlabelled text and then fine-tuned per task with minimal architectural change.
quality_notes: The arXiv page states no venue, so none is recorded here.
why_useful: Established the pretrain-then-fine-tune pattern that still shapes how NLP systems are built, and remains the clearest statement of why bidirectional context matters.
learning_outcomes: Explain masked language modelling as a pretraining objective
Describe the pretrain then fine-tune workflow
Distinguish encoder-only from decoder-only model families
abstract_summary: The abstract introduces BERT, a language representation model designed to pre-train deep bidirectional representations from unlabelled text by conditioning jointly on both left and right context in all layers. It states that the pretrained model can then be fine-tuned with one additional output layer to produce strong models for a range of tasks, including question answering and language inference, without substantial task-specific architectural changes.
key_idea: Conditioning on both directions at once, rather than left to right, is what makes a single pretrained encoder useful across many tasks. The practical consequence is that most teams stopped designing task-specific architectures.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
description: The paper introducing retrieval-augmented generation, combining a parametric sequence-to-sequence model with a non-parametric retrieved document index.
quality_notes: The original formulation differs substantially from what the industry now calls RAG. Useful for understanding where the term came from, not as an implementation guide.
why_useful: Reading the source clarifies that RAG was a specific architecture before it became a loose label, which cuts through a great deal of imprecise current writing.
learning_outcomes: Explain the original retrieval-augmented generation formulation
See how far current usage has drifted from the paper
abstract_summary: The abstract observes that large pretrained language models store factual knowledge in their parameters but access and manipulate it imprecisely, so they lag task-specific architectures on knowledge-intensive tasks, and that providing provenance and updating world knowledge remain open problems. It states that models with a differentiable access mechanism to explicit non-parametric memory can address this, and explores a general-purpose approach combining parametric and non-parametric memory.
key_idea: Separating what a model knows from where it can look is the point. Most of the engineering difficulty in a modern RAG system therefore sits in retrieval and evaluation rather than in generation.

title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
description: The paper introducing low-rank adaptation, which freezes pretrained weights and injects trainable low-rank matrices to reduce the cost of fine-tuning.
quality_notes: The arXiv page notes the draft has been revised with additional baselines and experiments, so check which version you are reading.
why_useful: The technique that made fine-tuning large models feasible without a research budget, and a rare case where linear algebra intuition maps directly onto a practical saving.
learning_outcomes: Explain low-rank adaptation and why it reduces cost
Reason about which layers to adapt and at what rank
Judge when adaptation beats prompting or retrieval
abstract_summary: The abstract describes the paradigm of large-scale pretraining followed by adaptation, and argues that full fine-tuning becomes less feasible as models grow, giving deployment of many independent 175-billion-parameter fine-tuned instances as an example of the cost. It proposes Low-Rank Adaptation, which freezes the pretrained weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each transformer layer, greatly reducing the number of trainable parameters for downstream tasks.
key_idea: The weight update needed to specialise a model appears to have far lower rank than the model itself, so it can be represented cheaply. That is an empirical claim about adaptation, not a general law, and it is worth reading the experiments rather than taking the framing on trust.

title: Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality
description: Extensions to the skip-gram model for learning word vectors, including subsampling of frequent words and negative sampling as an alternative to hierarchical softmax.
quality_notes: The arXiv page states no venue, so none is recorded.
why_useful: The source of the training tricks that made word embeddings practical, and the origin of intuitions about vector arithmetic that are still repeated second-hand today.
learning_outcomes: Explain negative sampling and why it replaces a full softmax
Describe how subsampling frequent words changes the learned vectors
abstract_summary: The abstract presents several extensions to the continuous skip-gram model that improve both vector quality and training speed. It states that subsampling frequent words gives a significant speedup and yields more regular representations, and describes negative sampling as a simple alternative to the hierarchical softmax.
key_idea: Much of what made early embeddings practical was training efficiency rather than a new theory of meaning. Reading it is a useful corrective to accounts that treat the resulting vector arithmetic as the discovery.

title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
description: Paper reporting that scaling language models substantially improves the ability to perform new tasks from a few examples or an instruction, without task-specific fine-tuning.
quality_notes: Long: the arXiv page records it at well over seventy pages. Read the framing and the evaluation sections rather than end to end.
why_useful: The paper that reframed prompting as the interface to a model, which is the assumption almost all current LLM application work is built on.
learning_outcomes: Explain few-shot prompting as distinct from fine-tuning
Reason about what scale did and did not change
abstract_summary: The abstract notes that pretraining followed by task-specific fine-tuning had produced substantial gains, but still required task-specific datasets of thousands of examples, whereas humans can generally perform a new language task from only a few examples or a simple instruction. It states that scaling up language models greatly improves task-agnostic few-shot performance.
key_idea: The claim is about scale changing how a model is used, not about the model reasoning. Reading the evaluation carefully is the fastest way to see how much of the popular account of this paper is actually in it.

title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
description: Paper showing that prompting a model with intermediate reasoning steps improves its performance on arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning tasks.
quality_notes: The word "reasoning" is doing a lot of work in the title. What is measured is task performance under a prompting change, which is not the same claim.
why_useful: The most cited source for a prompting technique in everyday use, and a good exercise in separating what a paper measured from what its title implies.
learning_outcomes: Apply chain-of-thought prompting deliberately rather than by habit
Distinguish a measured performance gain from a claim about reasoning
abstract_summary: The abstract explores how generating a chain of thought, described as a series of intermediate reasoning steps, improves the ability of large language models to perform complex reasoning. It states that such abilities emerge in sufficiently large models via chain-of-thought prompting, where a few such demonstrations are given as exemplars, and reports experiments on three large language models across arithmetic and commonsense tasks.
key_idea: The paper demonstrates a prompting technique and a scale threshold. Whether the intermediate text constitutes reasoning, or is a decoding pattern that happens to help, is not settled by the experiments it reports.
